"—Hijikata, is it,"
The commander Niimi Nishiki knit his brows.
It was odd. Why had the vice-commander Hijikata Toshizō, with whom he was ordinarily not on close terms, come here?
"Master Niimi. I seem to break in on your wine, but I have come, for the sake of the realm, to ask a decision of you."
"A decision?"
"Just so,"
Toshizō was, throughout, without expression.
"Of me?"
"Of course,"

"Hijikata, you are a vice-commander. Are you not a little hasty? In the Shinsengumi there are three who hold a commander's post—Master Serizawa, Kondō, and myself. For a light matter you may consult whichever commander you please. There is no need to come, of all places, to a spot like this."
"No—I have already consulted the other two."

Half a lie. But by now, at the barracks, Kondō should be sitting knee to knee with Serizawa, his trusted stalwarts ranged to left and right, in hard negotiation. So that Serizawa had been "consulted" was, by half, no lie.
"In any case,"
said Toshizō.
"this matter needs the assent of all three of you who are commanders of the Shinsengumi."
"Ah—if that is all, I have no objection. I'll leave it to you and yours."
"You will truly leave it to me, then?"
"I will,"
Niimi Nishiki waved a hand as if it were all a bother and took up his cooled cup. Watching his hand steadily, Toshizō,
"the matter is none other than this. I must ask Master Niimi to cut his belly, here and now."
"What—"
His hand flew to the sword at his side.
"Wait,"
Toshizō raised a hand.
"You gave your assent to it just now. A samurai does not speak twice."
"H-Hijikata,"
"I understand it well. The second's stroke this Hijikata Toshizō will take himself."
"Wh-why should I—"
"You cling to life, I daresay. Master Niimi Nishiki—the name once rang in Edo as a patriot of Mito. Come, like a samurai."
"I am asking the reason,"

"That you left to me, surely. From Master Serizawa, Master Kondō, and Master Niimi Nishiki—the ruling of these three commanders I have just now obtained. By that ruling of the three commanders, the Mito domain-leaver and rōnin Niimi Nishiki is ordered to cut his belly, for the offenses of extortion and the shaking-down of money and goods."
"Wait—I'll go back to the barracks,"
"The barracks of where?"
"You know very well. Mibu's,"

"Do you still take yourself for a commander of the Shinsengumi? That has already been stripped from you and struck off. And the one who so ruled was the commander Niimi Nishiki, who sat here until a moment ago. The person resembling him who sits here now is no longer a commander. A lawless, masterless rōnin, Niimi Nishiki.—"
"You—damn you,"
"Would you be cut down, Niimi Nishiki? I am trying to let you cut your belly like a samurai. That mercy comes from His Lordship the Aizu Middle Captain."
"Curse you—"
Rising onto his knees, he struck as he drew. He was drunk. His aim went wide.
Toshizō parried it, scabbard and all, with Akazawa Morito's sword that he held. The black-lacquered scabbard split, and the bare blade came out.
"This sword,"
Toshizō, taking his stance,
"was the wear of Akazawa Morito, whom you killed. With this sword I'll do you the office of second."
As he finished speaking, Okita Sōji was already come up behind.
At the same moment the papered door of the next room slid open with a rattle, and Saitō Hajime, Harada Sanosuke, and Nagakura Shinpachi showed their glum faces.
"Put down your sword,"
said Toshizō.
Niimi Nishiki's face went ghastly pale, and his knees could plainly be seen to shake, but the sword alone he would not put down.
Just then, of a sudden, someone stirred behind Niimi and made to bolt, pattering.
Wheeling as he turned, Niimi swept sidelong and cut the person down.

Blood flew, and a wrist dropped away with a flop. She fell with a thud and, in a sea of blood, began to shriek as if mad. It was the courtesan Niimi favored. Trying to flee, she had been cut by Niimi in his error.
Writhing, the woman cursed Niimi. Her face was like a she-demon's.

Niimi was plainly out of his mind. Seizing his sword all at once in a reverse grip, he ran it through the woman's breast. At the same moment he sat down hard on top of her body. The woman's corpse twitched.
"Hijikata—look,"
Niimi too was a man who had served as a commander of the Shinsengumi. Slowly he drew a paper from his breast and wound it about the blade.
"I'll take the second's stroke,"
Toshizō moved around behind. Niimi made to drive the blade into his belly. But his hand would not readily move, and he stared at a single point on the tatami with glittering eyes.
"Harada, lend him a hand,"
"Sir,"

Harada Sanosuke, too, was a man who, back home in Iyo Matsuyama, had once over some trifle begun to cut a belly there was no need to cut. Even now, across some three inches of his belly, ran the sewn scar of the wound.
"Your pardon,"
Clasping him from behind, with his great strength he gripped both Niimi's fists from above, holding them dead still, and,
"Master Niimi—thus,"
drove it in with a thrust. Niimi's upper body arched once, then pitched forward. In that instant, Toshizō's second's blade ran above Harada's head. The head fell forward.
Niimi was dead. At the same stroke, Serizawa Kamo's power was halved. In terms of a castle, the second bailey had fallen, and the keep alone remained.

As for that Serizawa: after Toshizō had gone off to Niimi, in a room of the Mibu barracks Kondō had pressed him hard with his stern doctrine of the-warrior's-code-first, and had driven him, for the moment, to the point of consenting to Niimi's punishment.
"Enough, enough,"
Serizawa wanted this fussy argument cut short and quickly. He meant to push off to Shimabara that night.
But Kondō clung on and would not let go.
"Master Serizawa, this is an important thing. Let me put it to you, to be sure: what do you suppose it is that governs the Shinsengumi?"
said Kondō. It was not Kondō's own reasoning but the reasoning Toshizō had taught him beforehand.
(What is he getting at?)
Such was the face Serizawa made. Himself, the head commander—who else, of course?
"Kondō—are you in your right mind,"
"I am,"
"Then say it,"
"The one who governs this corps is not Master Serizawa, nor Niimi, nor, of course, unworthy Kondō. No man with a body of flesh and limb is the ruler of this corps."
"What, then?"
"The warrior's code,"
said Kondō. Only he who, held up to the warrior's code, has nothing to be ashamed of can be a corpsman. He who goes against the warrior's code—that is death.
So Kondō said.
"Without it, there is no binding together these hot-blooded, high-passioned swordsmen gathered from every province into a single power beneath the imperial castle."
"Then let me ask,"
Serizawa put on a cold smile.
"the warrior's code, the warrior's code, you say—but what is this warrior's code of yours, Kondō?"
"Meaning?"

"You'll not know it, being of Tama peasant stock, but the Mito domain too has its warrior's code. It was beaten into us from childhood. Chōshū has it. Satsuma has it, Aizu has it, and all the other domains besides. Each differs a little, to be sure, by the temper of the domain; but the sum of it is that a samurai dies for his lord. That is what the warrior's code is. And who, pray, is the lord of the Shinsengumi?"
"The lord of the Shinsengumi—"
"Just so. The lord of the Shinsengumi is?"
"The warrior's code,"
"You don't understand. As I have just said, apart from a lord there is no such thing as the warrior's code. The Shinsengumi, having no lord, toward what is it to keep its code strict?"
Serizawa was of Mito, a domain of many debaters. Rough as he was, he knew how to argue.
"Well, Kondō?"
Kondō was stopped, and fell silent.
(A peasant-risen samurai.)
Such was the look on Serizawa's face.

That night Toshizō came back and reported to the two commanders, Serizawa and Kondō, the matter of Niimi Nishiki's seppuku. Hearing it, the veins all over Serizawa's face swelled with rage before their eyes.
"You—you did it?"

Serizawa had reckoned it all mere talk. But the peasant swordsman of South Tama in Bushū before his eyes was nothing at all like a Mito man whose arguments collapsed into words. Coolly, had the fellow not gone and done it? Serizawa felt now as if he had met a race of men he had never seen before. Not Serizawa alone: warriors such as Kondō and Hijikata had, in all likelihood, never been since the samurai of Japan began.
Serizawa kicked back his seat and rose.
Presently he came in, followed by three corpsmen of his following from the Mito days.
Jokin, Noguchi Kenji.
Jokin, Hirayama Gorō.
Jokin, Hirama Jūsuke.
All were Mito domain-leavers, and of the same school as Serizawa, the Shintō Munen-ryū.
The three seated themselves ringing Serizawa. Their looks were menacing.

Hirayama Gorō, for one, had loosened his sword in its mouth. His chin up, he let his head drop a little to the left. This was the man's habit when he was about to cut someone. "Gorō the one-eyed," they called him. His left eye was gone—crushed by a burn. The habit came of that.
Serizawa spoke.
"Kondō, Hijikata. Once more, let me hear the reason for Niimi Nishiki's seppuku."
Kondō held his tongue.
Toshizō smiled.
"Unpreparedness in the warrior's code,"

Neither Toshizō nor Kondō had ever, as Serizawa said, belonged to any domain. Just for that, the two of them held a vivid ideal image of what a warrior was. Unlike the shogunal retainers and the domains' samurai, who had inherited three hundred years of idle, back-scratching ease—
"the warrior,"
the very sound of the word held for them a freshness.
And not that alone.

They were of Bushū Tama. The Three Tama were shogunal-domain land, and all three districts were peasantry. But before the Warring States age, going back as far as the era of the Genji and the Heike, this land had been the breeding-ground of the Bandō warriors, whose hardihood was the boast of the realm. Naturally the ideal of the warrior's code these two held was the old warriors of Bandō.
Not the soft, weak warrior of the Edo age.
"Master Serizawa, do you not understand it,"
said Toshizō.
"Master Niimi, held up to the warrior's code, was gravely unprepared in it. That is the sole reason for the seppuku. And at the same time—"
"At the same time?"
"even Master Serizawa, should he go against the warrior's code, then—seppuku, of course; failing that, the severing of the head."
"What—"
Hirayama rose.
"Hirayama,"
Toshizō slowly raised a hand.
"Do you mean to make war within the corps? Let me clap my hands here, and our comrades from the Edo days will come pouring in on the instant."
The Serizawa faction withdrew.
From that night they ought to have plotted revenge; but they chose another road. They sank into drink and women. Serizawa's wild conduct grew worse than before.

Serizawa, commander of the Shinsengumi, was in Kyoto very nearly an all-powerful king. On the road, if a townsman did him a discourtesy, he cut him down. Taking a fancy to a common corpsman's mistress, for the one reason that the man was in his way he lured that corpsman—Sasaki Aijirō—to his death. He had long been ordering silks from the Hishiya, a draper at Shijō-Horikawa, and, paying not a mon, was being pressed for it. The dun was sometimes the head clerk, but sometimes it was the Hishiya's kept woman who came. Oume, she was called. Her he took by force; and not only did he leave the debt unpaid but lived with Oume at the barracks in a wanton life, all but cohabiting, till it became the talk of the townhouses about Horikawa.
Toshizō held his tongue. Kondō too held his tongue. But the plan was moving steadily on. The men to strike had already been decided.
Kondō Isami, Hijikata Toshizō, Okita Sōji, Inoue Genzaburō—a bare four.

Nagakura Shinpachi and Tōdō Heisuke were not chosen. These two were comrades from the Edo days and had shared in every secret of the Kondō line; but Toshizō was cautious still. They were not of the Tennen Rishin-ryū.

Tōdō Heisuke was of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū, Nagakura Shinpachi of the Shintō Munen-ryū. Having once been house-guests at Kondō's dōjō on the Kohinata heights in Edo, they ranked as hatamoto to Kondō; but they were not, so to speak, hatamoto since the Mikawa days. On consideration, they were left out.
The deed would be done by the Tama party. By the hand of the four Tennen Rishin-ryū men who had scraped that poor dōjō along. To Toshizō, these comrades alone could be trusted.
"Still—it's a little uncertain,"
said Kondō. If it was to be done, he wished to slaughter the whole Serizawa faction at a single blow. With too few, there was a danger of leaving some undone.
"Toshi, what do you say,"
So saying, Kondō, on his writing-practice sheet,
"Sa,"
wrote the one character.
It was Harada Sanosuke.
"Ah—that's good,"
Toshizō nodded. A man like a fierce dog; and just for that, his obedience to Kondō had something animal in it.
With Toshizō present, Kondō called Harada Sanosuke. Through Toshizō's mouth he drew from him, offhand, what he thought of Serizawa these days.
"A fine, bold fellow,"
Harada laughed, a dry cackle.

Kondō made a surprised face. Come to think of it, Harada was a man of the same stamp as Serizawa. The one difference was that Harada, having risen from the low estate of a season-and-half-season hired footman of the Matsuyama domain, and having known hard usage from boyhood, was somewhere quick to tears.
"Harada—between ourselves, I mean to cut down Serizawa Kamo alone,"
said Kondō.
Even Harada was startled, as well he might be.
"You, Master—alone?"
"That's right. But Hijikata here is against it. He says he'll join in himself."
"That won't do,"
Harada was a simple man.

"Hijikata is right. It's not Commander Serizawa alone, mind. First off, there's Hirayama. And Noguchi and Hirama, clever devils both. Should the least harm come to you, Master—what becomes of the Shinsengumi? Hijikata—"
"Hm?"
"Talk him round, please. Master Kondō seems to think the life is his own and his alone."
"Understood,"
Toshizō, unusually for this man, showed a bright smile.
"Harada—let's do it,"
"That we will,"

Of any debate over the rights and wrongs of cutting down the head commander, this man's head held nothing. It may be that the Shinsengumi's "warrior's code" as Toshizō conceived it, sought in an example, was a man like Harada Sanosuke.
Harada was close-mouthed.
Until the day came, neither Kondō nor Toshizō made the matter a subject of talk.
Bunkyū 3, the eighteenth day of the ninth month: after sundown, rain.
From late in the hour of the Dragon it turned to a downpour laced with a high wind. The temporary bridge at Kōjinguchi on the Kamo River was washed away, so it must have been a heavy rain indeed.
At midnight Serizawa came back to barracks drunk from Shimabara and lay with Oume, who had waited in his room. The two coupled naked and so fell asleep.
Hirayama and Hirama, who had gone with him to Shimabara, fell asleep too, each in a separate room. The Serizawa faction's lodging was, by this time, the Yagi Gennojō house.
Across a single road stood the Kondō faction's lodging, the Maekawa Sōji house.
About half past twelve in the morning, five Tennen Rishin-ryū men, Harada Sanosuke added to their number, fell upon the Yagi Gennojō house like a gust of wind.
Oume, killed instantly.

The first stroke at Serizawa was Okita's; as he tried to rise, Toshizō put in the second stroke; and when even so he rolled out onto the veranda and stumbled over a writing-desk, Kondō's Kotetsu drove straight down into his breast.
Hirayama Gorō was lying with Kichiei, a Shimabara harlot; Harada Sanosuke, bursting in, first kicked Kichiei's pillow.
"Run,"
Harada had bedded this woman before. Kichiei cried out and, knocking down the sliding door, tumbled out.
Hirayama, waking with a start, crawled quickly and stretched a hand toward his sword.
There Harada cut him.
It struck the shoulder-blade and did not cut deep enough. Harada, in the pitch dark, boldly leaned in to look.
With an "Ah!" Hirayama reared his head like a striking snake.
There Harada struck. The head flew as far as the alcove and rolled.
Hirama Jūsuke fled.
Noguchi Kenji was absent.
At the end of that year, on the twenty-eighth, Noguchi cut his belly for "unpreparedness in the warrior's code." The Serizawa faction was annihilated.
